title: Gut Wisdom: Managing Digestive Health & IBS
summary: A comprehensive, evidence-based CBT program for managing irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) and improving digestive health. This program addresses the gut-brain connection, teaches stress management techniques for digestive symptoms, and provides practical tools for symptom tracking and trigger identification. Learn to work with your digestive system, not against it.

modules.title: Module 1 • Understanding the Gut-Brain Connection
modules.overview: We begin by exploring the fascinating connection between your brain and your gut—the 'second brain' in your digestive system. You will learn about the 'Enteric Nervous System'—the network of neurons in your gut that communicates directly with your brain. We explore how stress, anxiety, and emotions directly impact digestive function. Understanding this connection is the first step to managing symptoms. The concept of 'Visceral Sensitivity' is introduced—how people with IBS often have heightened sensitivity to normal digestive sensations. You will learn about common IBS symptoms and subtypes (IBS-C, IBS-D, IBS-M) and how they manifest. We address the 'IBS Cycle'—how symptoms create anxiety, which creates more symptoms, creating more anxiety. Finally, we set the foundation: Managing IBS requires addressing both the physical (gut) and psychological (brain) aspects.
takeaways: Your gut and brain are in constant communication—what affects one affects the other.
Stress and anxiety directly impact digestive symptoms.
IBS is real, manageable, and not 'all in your head'—but your head does play a role.
Understanding the gut-brain connection empowers you to intervene effectively.
exercises: The Gut-Brain Journal: For one week, track your digestive symptoms alongside your stress levels and emotions. Notice patterns: Do symptoms correlate with stress or mood?
The Symptom Inventory: List all your digestive symptoms. Rate their frequency and severity (1-10). Which symptoms are most disruptive to your life?
The IBS Cycle Map: Draw your personal cycle: What triggers your symptoms? How do symptoms affect your thoughts? How do thoughts affect symptoms? Identify entry points for intervention.
homework: Continue the Gut-Brain Journal for 7 days. Look for connections between stress, emotions, and digestive symptoms.
Research your IBS subtype (if diagnosed). Understand how it typically manifests. This knowledge helps you recognize patterns.
Practice one stress reduction technique daily (deep breathing, meditation, gentle movement). Notice any impact on digestive symptoms.

modules.title: Module 2 • Stress Management for Digestive Symptoms
modules.overview: This module focuses specifically on stress management techniques that directly impact digestive health. We explore 'The Relaxation Response'—how activating the parasympathetic nervous system calms the digestive system. You will learn 'Gut-Directed Hypnotherapy' principles—using relaxation and imagery to calm digestive symptoms. The concept of 'Diaphragmatic Breathing' is introduced—breathing techniques that activate the vagus nerve and calm the gut. We address 'Progressive Muscle Relaxation' adapted for digestive health—releasing tension in the abdomen and throughout the body. You will create a 'Digestive Calm Toolkit'—specific techniques you can use when symptoms flare. Finally, we practice 'Preventive Stress Management'—regular practice to prevent symptoms, not just manage them when they occur.
takeaways: Stress management directly impacts digestive symptoms.
The relaxation response can calm the gut-brain connection.
Regular practice is more effective than occasional use.
You have tools to calm your digestive system through your mind.
exercises: The Diaphragmatic Breathing Practice: Learn belly breathing. Practice 10 minutes daily for one week. Notice how it affects your digestive symptoms.
The Gut Calm Imagery: Create a visualization of your digestive system working smoothly. Practice this daily. Use it when symptoms flare.
Build Your Digestive Calm Toolkit: List 5-7 techniques that help calm your digestive symptoms (breathing, imagery, gentle movement, etc.). Practice each this week.
homework: Practice diaphragmatic breathing for 10 minutes, twice daily. Track any changes in symptoms.
Use gut-directed imagery when symptoms flare. Notice if it helps reduce intensity or duration.
Try progressive muscle relaxation, focusing on releasing tension in your abdomen. Practice 3 times this week.

modules.title: Module 3 • Symptom Tracking & Trigger Identification
modules.overview: This module teaches systematic approaches to identifying what triggers your digestive symptoms. We introduce 'The FODMAP Concept'—understanding how certain carbohydrates can trigger IBS symptoms (this is educational, not a strict diet plan). You will learn to create a 'Symptom & Food Diary'—tracking what you eat, when you eat, stress levels, and symptoms to identify patterns. The concept of 'Trigger Categories' is explained—foods, stress, hormones, sleep, and other factors that can affect symptoms. We address 'Pattern Recognition'—learning to identify your personal triggers through careful observation. You will practice 'Elimination & Reintroduction' principles—systematically testing foods to identify sensitivities (under guidance if needed). Finally, we create a 'Personal Trigger Profile'—your unique map of what affects your digestive health.
takeaways: Everyone's triggers are different; identifying yours is key.
Tracking symptoms alongside potential triggers reveals patterns.
Food is one factor, but stress, sleep, and other factors also matter.
Systematic tracking is more effective than guessing.
exercises: Start Your Symptom & Food Diary: Track for 7 days: meals, timing, stress levels (1-10), sleep quality, and symptoms (type, severity, timing). Look for patterns.
The Trigger Categories Assessment: List potential triggers in each category: Foods, Stress, Sleep, Hormones, Eating Patterns, Other. Which categories seem most relevant?
The Pattern Analysis: After one week of tracking, identify 2-3 potential patterns. What seems to correlate with symptoms? What seems protective?
homework: Continue your Symptom & Food Diary for 2 more weeks. The longer you track, the clearer patterns become.
Test one hypothesis: If you suspect a food triggers symptoms, try eliminating it for 3-5 days. Notice any changes. Then reintroduce and observe.
Identify one non-food trigger (stress, sleep, etc.) and experiment with managing it. Notice impact on symptoms.

modules.title: Module 4 • Dietary Modifications & The FODMAP Approach
modules.overview: This module provides education about dietary approaches to managing IBS, with a focus on the FODMAP diet as a tool, not a life sentence. We explore 'What Are FODMAPs?'—understanding fermentable carbohydrates that can trigger symptoms in sensitive individuals. You will learn about 'The FODMAP Process'—elimination, reintroduction, and personalization phases (ideally with guidance). The concept of 'Portion Sizes' is introduced—sometimes it's not the food, but the amount that triggers symptoms. We address 'Eating Patterns'—how the way you eat (rushed, stressed, large meals) affects digestion. You will learn 'Practical Meal Planning'—making dietary modifications sustainable and realistic. Finally, we practice 'Flexible Adherence'—using dietary knowledge as a tool, not a rigid rulebook.
takeaways: Dietary modifications can help, but extreme restriction is unsustainable.
FODMAPs are a tool for identification, not a permanent diet.
How you eat matters as much as what you eat.
Personalization is key—what works for others might not work for you.
exercises: The FODMAP Education: Research FODMAPs. List high-FODMAP foods in each category (fructose, lactose, etc.). Understand the concept, but don't start elimination without guidance.
The Eating Pattern Audit: Track for 3 days: meal timing, portion sizes, eating speed, stress during meals. Notice patterns: Do rushed or stressed meals correlate with symptoms?
Create 3 Dietary Swaps: Identify 3 foods that might trigger symptoms. Find lower-FODMAP or alternative options. Try one swap this week.
homework: If considering FODMAP elimination, consult a dietitian or healthcare provider first. Don't do it alone—it requires guidance.
Experiment with eating patterns: Try smaller, more frequent meals for 3 days. Or try eating more slowly. Notice impact on symptoms.
Add one gut-friendly food this week (e.g., oatmeal, bananas, ginger tea). Notice how it feels.

modules.title: Module 5 • Cognitive Restructuring for Digestive Anxiety
modules.overview: This module addresses the anxiety and catastrophic thinking that often accompanies IBS and digestive issues. We explore 'Digestive Anxiety'—the fear and worry about symptoms, bathroom access, and social situations. You will learn to identify 'Catastrophic Thoughts' about digestive symptoms (e.g., 'I'll never be able to leave the house' or 'This will never get better'). The concept of 'Cognitive Restructuring' is introduced—challenging unhelpful thoughts and replacing them with balanced perspectives. We address 'Safety Behaviors'—avoidance and other behaviors that reduce anxiety short-term but maintain it long-term. You will practice 'Exposure & Response Prevention' principles—gradually facing feared situations to reduce anxiety. Finally, we create a 'Digestive Anxiety Toolkit'—strategies for managing worry and fear about symptoms.
takeaways: Anxiety about symptoms can worsen symptoms—it's a cycle.
Catastrophic thoughts are usually exaggerated; challenging them helps.
Avoidance maintains anxiety; gradual exposure reduces it.
You can manage digestive anxiety, which helps manage symptoms.
exercises: The Catastrophic Thought Record: When you have anxious thoughts about digestive symptoms, write them down. Challenge them: 'Is this thought helpful? Is it true? What's a more balanced thought?'
The Safety Behavior Audit: List all things you avoid or do to prevent symptoms (avoiding certain foods, staying home, always knowing bathroom locations, etc.). Which maintain anxiety?
Create Your Exposure Hierarchy: List 5-7 situations you avoid due to digestive anxiety. Rank them by difficulty. Start with the easiest. Plan gradual exposure.
homework: Challenge 3 catastrophic thoughts this week. Write them down. Find balanced alternatives. Notice how this affects your anxiety.
Reduce one safety behavior this week. If you always check for bathrooms, try going somewhere without checking first. Notice what happens.
Complete one item from your exposure hierarchy. Start small. Build confidence gradually.

modules.title: Module 6 • Integration & Long-Term Management
modules.overview: The final module focuses on integrating all components—stress management, trigger identification, dietary modifications, and cognitive strategies—into a sustainable approach. We explore 'The Comprehensive Approach'—how all pieces work together to manage IBS. You will create a 'Digestive Health Maintenance Plan'—a personalized system for managing symptoms long-term. The concept of 'Symptom Management vs. Cure' is addressed—IBS may be chronic, but symptoms can be well-managed. We address 'Setback Management'—how to handle flare-ups and periods when symptoms are worse. You will learn 'Problem-Solving Skills'—systematic approaches to addressing challenges as they arise. Finally, we write a 'Digestive Health Commitment'—a personal statement of your values and intentions for long-term digestive wellness.
takeaways: Managing IBS is a long-term process, not a quick fix.
All components work together—stress management, diet, cognitive strategies.
Setbacks are normal; persistence and self-compassion are key.
You have the tools to manage your digestive health effectively.
exercises: Create Your Digestive Health Maintenance Plan: Integrate stress management, trigger awareness, dietary choices, and cognitive strategies into a weekly routine. Make it sustainable.
The Setback Response Plan: Write down: 'If I have a symptom flare-up, I will...' Create a specific action plan for managing setbacks.
Write Your Digestive Health Commitment: In 200-300 words, write your personal statement about digestive health. Include your values, intentions, and how you'll manage IBS long-term.
homework: Implement your Digestive Health Maintenance Plan for 4 weeks. Adjust as needed. Notice what works and what needs refinement.
Continue tracking symptoms periodically (weekly or monthly) to identify new patterns or triggers.
Review your Digestive Health Commitment monthly. Use it as a reminder of your approach and intentions.
Celebrate your progress. Every symptom managed, every fear faced, every tool used—it all adds up. You're taking care of your digestive health.

aiSupport.systemPrompt: Help the user apply one concrete module step at a time. Do not diagnose. Escalate urgent safety concerns to emergency care.
